title: The day the scroll was read aloud

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever joined something already going, a class, a team, a family, and had to find your place?
options: then this story might help. listen.
then you know the feeling. listen.
then listen. this one is about stepping in.

steps.line: Long ago, after years in exile, the people came home to Jerusalem. One autumn day, they all gathered as one, in the square before the Water Gate.
Ezra the scribe climbed onto a tall wooden platform and opened the scroll in front of everyone. When he opened it, all the people stood up.

steps.q: Ezra begins to read. How long do you think he reads?
steps.why: About six hours, Nehemiah says, and everyone listened closely the whole time.

steps.line: He read from early morning until midday. Men and women, and everyone old enough to understand, listened.
As he read, the Levites, the teachers, stood among the people. They read clearly, and gave the sense, so the people understood the reading.

steps.q: Why might these people have needed help to understand their own Torah?
o: After exile, many spoke Aramaic day to day
Only priests had been taught to read it
Ezra was reading far too quickly
steps.why: After decades in Babylon, many spoke Aramaic at home, and the Torah’s old Hebrew could be hard going. So the teachers explained as he read.

steps.line: The people began to weep. But they were told: don’t grieve. Go, eat rich food, drink something sweet, and send portions to anyone who has nothing ready.

steps.q: The people wept as they heard the Torah. Why were they told to stop, and go feast?
o: There was no time for both that day
It was a holy day, meant for joy
Weeping in public broke the law
steps.why: It was the first day of the seventh month, today’s Rosh Hashanah. “The joy of the Lord is your strength,” they were told.

steps.line: Today, one portion of the Torah, a parsha, is read every Shabbat, with shorter readings on Monday and Thursday mornings. The rabbis credited Ezra with shaping them.
steps.label: today

steps.line: Communities read it in different ways. Orthodox synagogues read the full portion each week. Many Reform and some Conservative ones read part of it, on a three-year cycle.
steps.label: today

steps.q: When the yearly reading reaches the last words of Deuteronomy, what happens next?
o: The scroll rests until the new year
They start again at Genesis, that day
They read the whole thing again, fast
steps.why: On Simchat Torah, communities read the last lines and the first ones back to back, often dancing with the scrolls. The circle never stops.

say: here’s what i love. you don’t start the torah on page one when you’re ready. you find out where everyone is this week, and you step in there.
the rabbis even suggested a way at home: read the week’s portion twice, and once in translation. just like the teachers in ezra’s crowd, making sure people understood.

steps.q: The rabbis said “read clearly” here meant translating the reading. What does that say about how Torah should be read?
steps.why: The goal is understanding. Hebrew, and a translation beside it, so the words reach you.

today.say: look up this week’s torah portion: its name, and one line from it. that’s it. you’ve just stepped into a reading that has been going around the world for centuries.
options: then you’re in the cycle. welcome.
it’ll be there. it’s always going.

tomorrow.line: next, the stories begin, at the very first word of the scroll. and a letter that waited twenty-six generations for its turn.
